fatal_errors: The proposed Mo-to-V substitution does not reconstruct the target intervention, which was cold rolling followed by controlled annealing of a Mo-lean Nb35Zr26Ti19Hf15Mo5 alloy.
No supporting prior evidence is cited despite the explicit request for it.

The central assertion that V substitution will preserve yield strength within 10% while increasing plasticity is speculative and is not supported by strengthening calculations, prior alloy data, or mechanistic measurements.
explanation: The hypothesis is responsive to the stated strength–plasticity problem and proposes a clear single compositional intervention, operating window, quantitative outcome criterion, and reasonably discriminating composition-series experiment. However, it differs fundamentally from the hidden target in material composition, processing route, loading mode, structural mediator, and expected trends. The target used deformation processing and recovery/recrystallization to tune tensile strength and elongation, whereas the generated hypothesis invokes reduced electronegativity mismatch through V substitution under compression. Its mechanism is chemically plausible at a qualitative level, but the link from lower electronegativity mismatch to improved dislocation mobility—and especially to retention of nearly all of the Mo-derived strength—is unsubstantiated. The falsification experiment can test performance, although matched grain size, segregation, porosity, and processing history would also be needed to attribute any change specifically to chemistry. With no prior evidence and no direct support for the quantitative prediction, this is an unsupported alternative rather than a reconstruction.
